blocks.text: 1. Introduction
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442416930-96988048.png

Picture a spreadsheet of everyone’s salary at a fifty person startup. Forty nine people earn somewhere between 60,000 and 140,000 dollars a year. One person, the founder, earns 4 million dollars because of a stock payout that year. If you compute the average salary across all fifty rows, you get a number that describes literally nobody at the company. That single row just wrecked your summary statistic. That is an outlier, a value that sits far enough away from the rest of the data that it distorts anything you try to compute from the whole group.

Outliers show up everywhere real data gets collected: sensor glitches, typos during manual entry, a genuinely rare event, a system bug that logs a timestamp as year zero. Before you can decide what to do about one, you first need a reliable way to actually find it. That is what this lesson is about, using pandas and NumPy to detect outliers in a column of numbers, and then making the harder call of what to actually do once you have found one.

Outliers matter more in machine learning than they do in a typical spreadsheet, because a model does not just glance at your data, it learns from it. A single extreme value can badly skew a mean, and that skewed mean often becomes an input to something else downstream: a normalization step, a filled in missing value, a threshold. The distortion does not stay contained, it propagates.

items: Linear regression, where the fitted line gets pulled toward extreme points because the loss function squares every error, and one huge error counts a lot.
Anything trained with gradient descent, where one unusually large input can produce one unusually large gradient update and destabilize training.
Distance based methods like k-nearest neighbors or k-means, where a single feature with a huge outlier value can dominate the distance calculation and drown out every other feature.
Any preprocessing step built on the mean or the standard deviation, since both of those get pulled around by extreme values before the model ever sees the data.

blocks.text: None of this means an outlier is automatically a mistake. Sometimes it is a genuine, important, rare event that you actually want your model to know about. Sometimes it really is a data entry error, an age of 200 or a price that went negative, and it needs to be fixed before it poisons anything downstream. Detecting an outlier and deciding what to do about it are two separate steps, and this lesson covers both, starting with detection.

Two detection methods do almost all of the work in practice: the interquartile range rule and the z-score rule. Both give you a rule for flagging a value as unusual, and you will see that they do not always agree with each other, which turns out to be a genuinely useful thing to know.
2. The IQR Method
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442416931-370702157.png

The interquartile range method, IQR for short, is the same rule that a box plot draws as its whiskers, even if you never actually draw the box plot. It is simple, it does not assume your data follows any particular distribution, and pandas gives you everything you need to compute it in two lines.
2.1 Quartiles and the Interquartile Range

A quartile splits sorted data into four equal chunks. Q1, the first quartile, is the value below which 25 percent of your data falls. Q3, the third quartile, is the value below which 75 percent of your data falls. If you have already seen the statistical operations lesson, this is exactly the same idea as a percentile: Q1 is just the 25th percentile and Q3 is just the 75th percentile, computed with the same quantile() method.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

prices = pd.Series([12, 14, 13, 15, 12, 16, 15, 14, 250, 13, 15, 14])

q1 = prices.quantile(0.25)
q3 = prices.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

print(q1, q3, iqr)

blocks.text: The interquartile range, or IQR, is just Q3 minus Q1. It is the width of the middle 50 percent of your data, the chunk sitting between the first and third quartile. Because it only looks at the middle half, a handful of extreme values at either end barely move it at all, which is exactly the property that makes it useful for finding those extreme values in the first place.
2.2 The 1.5 Times IQR Rule

Once you have the IQR, the classic rule for flagging outliers is to build a lower and upper boundary around it. Anything below Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR, or anything above Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR, gets flagged as an outlier.

code.content:
lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

outliers = prices[(prices < lower_bound) | (prices > upper_bound)]
print(lower_bound, upper_bound)
print(outliers)

blocks.text: That 1.5 multiplier is not derived from anything deep, it is a convention that turned out to work well in practice and stuck. Tighten it to 1.0 and you flag more values as outliers. Loosen it to 3.0 and you flag fewer. It is worth remembering that this number is a dial you can turn, not a law of nature.

blocks.title: Why this looks familiar from box plots
blocks.content: If you have ever looked at a box plot, the whiskers extending above and below the box stop at exactly these two boundaries, Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR on the bottom and Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR on the top. Any point plotted beyond a whisker is the box plot drawing this exact rule for you. Knowing the rule means you can read a box plot correctly even without ever calling a single plotting function.

blocks.text: 3. The Z-Score Method
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417249-816866230.png

The z-score method asks a different question than IQR does. Instead of looking at quartiles, it asks how many standard deviations a value sits away from the mean. It is a genuinely useful second opinion, and later in this lesson you will see it does not always agree with the IQR rule.
3.1 What a Z-Score Measures

A z-score is computed as the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation. A z-score of 0 means the value sits exactly at the mean. A z-score of 2 means the value sits two standard deviations above the mean. A negative z-score means the value sits below the mean.

code.content:
mean = prices.mean()
std = prices.std()

z_scores = (prices - mean) / std
print(z_scores.round(2))

blocks.text: The sign tells you which direction, above or below the mean, and the magnitude tells you how far. A z-score of 0.3 is unremarkable, most of your data will sit somewhere between negative 1 and positive 1. A z-score of 4 is genuinely rare if your data is roughly normally distributed.
3.2 The Z-Score Threshold

A common threshold is to flag anything with an absolute z-score above 3. In a roughly normal distribution, about 99.7 percent of values fall within 3 standard deviations of the mean, so a value beyond that point is rare enough to be worth a second look.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Threshold","Roughly how much data falls inside it","Effect"],"rows":[["2","About 95 percent","Flags more values, a looser definition of typical"],["2.5","About 99 percent","A middle ground some teams use"],["3","About 99.7 percent","The most common default, flags fewer values"]]}

blocks.text: 3.3 The Circularity Caveat

Here is the catch. A z-score is computed using the mean and the standard deviation of the same column you are trying to check for outliers. Both the mean and the standard deviation are themselves sensitive to extreme values, the exact same sensitivity that made outliers worth worrying about back in the introduction. One huge value can drag the mean up and inflate the standard deviation, and once the standard deviation is inflated, that same huge value, and any other moderately unusual value, can end up looking artificially normal in z-score terms.

blocks.title: This is the same robustness idea from mean versus median
blocks.content: You have likely run into this before: the mean is pulled around by extreme values while the median mostly ignores them. That is why the missing value imputation lesson in this module often recommends filling missing numbers with a median rather than a mean on skewed data, the mean is already compromised. The z-score method inherits that exact same weakness, because it leans on the mean and the standard deviation, not the more robust median. On a heavily skewed column, treat a z-score result with a bit of suspicion.

blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: IQR versus Z-Score on the Same Data

blocks.alt: Worked Example: IQR versus Z-Score on the Same Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417251-385983578.png
Here is a small dataset of customer ages where the two methods genuinely disagree. Twelve customers, most of them clustered in their early twenties, one who is 34, and one clear anomaly at 95.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

ages = pd.Series([22, 24, 23, 25, 22, 26, 24, 23, 25, 24, 34, 95])

q1, q3 = ages.quantile(0.25), ages.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower_bound, upper_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr

iqr_outliers = ages[(ages < lower_bound) | (ages > upper_bound)]
print(lower_bound, upper_bound)   # 19.625 28.625
print(iqr_outliers)
# 10    34
# 11    95

z_scores = (ages - ages.mean()) / ages.std()
z_outliers = ages[z_scores.abs() > 3]

print(z_scores.round(2))
print(z_outliers)
# 11    95

blocks.text: Run both methods and you get two different answers. The IQR rule flags both 34 and 95. The z-score rule, at the common threshold of 3, only flags 95.

34 is exactly the circularity problem from the last section playing out with real numbers. That single 95 pulls the mean up to about 30.6 and inflates the standard deviation to about 20.5, both computed from data that already includes the very outlier distorting them. Against that inflated spread, 34 only works out to a z-score of about 0.17, unremarkable. But relative to the tight cluster of ages sitting in the low twenties, which is what the IQR rule actually looks at, 34 is clearly out of place. Neither method is wrong exactly, they are just measuring distance from center using two different, and in this case disagreeing, definitions of center and spread.
5. Is It Actually Wrong? The Judgment Call

blocks.alt: Is It Actually Wrong? The Judgment Call
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417251-623555562.png

Everything up to this point has been about detection, finding candidates. Neither IQR nor z-score tells you whether a flagged value is actually a problem. That is a judgment call, and it depends entirely on what the data represents, not on which statistical rule flagged it.
5.1 Genuine Rare Events

Sometimes an extreme value is exactly what it looks like, a real, rare thing that actually happened. Removing it would not clean your data, it would throw away real signal that your model might genuinely need to learn from.

items: A record breaking sale during a once a year flash promotion.
A genuinely record setting measurement, like the fastest lap time ever recorded at a race track.
An unusually tall or unusually short person’s height, in a dataset built from the general population.
A traffic spike on the one day your app got featured somewhere popular.

blocks.text: 5.2 Data Entry Errors

Other times, a flagged value is simply wrong, a mistake introduced somewhere between the real world and your dataframe. These are the ones you generally do want to fix or remove, because leaving them in place teaches your model something that is not true.

items: A price entered as a negative number.
A percentage value of 150 in a column that should top out at 100.
A default timestamp from the year 1970 because a field was left blank and a system filled in a placeholder.

blocks.text: 5.3 Domain Knowledge Decides

Notice that nothing about the number itself tells you which of these two categories it falls into. A value of 95 in the ages example earlier could be a data entry mistake, or it could be a legitimate customer, plenty of 95 year olds sign up for things. The only way to actually know is to look at the context: check the source system, check whether other fields in that same row make sense together, ask someone who understands the business. Statistics can flag a candidate. Only domain knowledge can turn that candidate into a verdict.

blocks.title: An outlier is not automatically wrong
blocks.content: It is tempting to treat every flagged value as a bug to be squashed. Resist that instinct. A detection rule like IQR or z-score has no idea what your data actually represents, it is just counting distance. Deleting every flagged row without checking first is a great way to quietly delete the most interesting, most informative rows in your entire dataset.

blocks.text: 6. Handling a Confirmed Outlier
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417252-861762847.png

Once you have decided a flagged value genuinely needs handling, whether because it is a confirmed error or because it is a legitimate extreme value that is still causing problems downstream, you have three broad options.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","What it does","When it fits well"],"rows":[["Remove the row","Drops the record from the dataset entirely","The value is a confirmed error and there is no way to recover the true underlying value"],["Cap it with clip","Pulls the value in to a boundary, keeps the row in place","You want to keep the row but stop one extreme value from dominating a mean sensitive calculation"],["Use a robust approach instead","Leaves the raw value untouched and picks a model or preprocessing step that is not thrown off by extremes","The value might be genuine signal and you would rather not touch the raw data at all"]]}

blocks.text: 6.1 Removing the Row

The simplest option is to drop the row. This is the right call for confirmed errors where you cannot recover the true value, an age of 200 with no way to check the real one, or a duplicate sensor glitch reading. It is also the most destructive option, since the row is simply gone, so reach for it only once you are confident the value is genuinely wrong.
6.2 Capping with .clip()

.clip() takes a different approach: instead of deleting the row, it pulls the extreme value in to a fixed boundary and leaves everything else about the row untouched. This keeps your row count and every other column intact, while stopping that one value from dragging a mean or a model weight around.

code.content:
capped = ages.clip(lower=lower_bound, upper=upper_bound)
print(capped)
# the 95 becomes 28.625, the upper bound, everything else stays the same

blocks.text: 6.3 Choosing a Robust Approach Instead

Sometimes the better move is to change nothing about the data at all, and instead pick tools that are naturally less sensitive to extreme values. Use the median instead of the mean when filling missing values or summarizing a skewed column. Use a tree based model like a random forest or gradient boosted trees instead of linear regression, since trees split on thresholds rather than fitting a line that every point pulls on. Use a robust scaler that centers and scales using the median and the IQR instead of the mean and standard deviation.
7. Worked Example: A Sales Dataset With Both Kinds of Outlier
Here is a small orders table where the IQR rule flags two rows, and the two flagged rows turn out to need completely different treatment. Most orders sit somewhere between 120 and 160 dollars.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": range(1, 13),
    "amount": [120, 150, 135, 142, 128, -45, 160, 138, 155, 145, 15200, 133],
})

q1 = sales["amount"].quantile(0.25)
q3 = sales["amount"].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

flagged = sales[(sales["amount"] < lower_bound) | (sales["amount"] > upper_bound)]
print(lower_bound, upper_bound)   # 102.5 180.5
print(flagged)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Order","Amount","What it turned out to be"],"rows":[["Order 6","-45","A data entry error, a price cannot be negative"],["Order 11","15200","A real, confirmed wholesale order"]]}

blocks.text: Order 6 needs no investigation at all. A negative price is not a rare, legitimate business event, it is a broken record, most likely a sign flipped during entry or an export bug. It gets fixed or dropped.

code.content:
# a negative price cannot be real, drop the row
sales = sales[sales["amount"] >= 0]

blocks.text: Order 11 is different. A quick check against the order records confirms it: a real customer placed a genuine bulk wholesale order for 15200 dollars that week. Dropping this row would delete a completely true, and honestly pretty important, data point. Instead of removing it, cap a copy of the column used for anything mean sensitive, while keeping the original amount intact for reporting.

code.content:
# keep the real value for reporting, but protect a
# mean sensitive downstream step with a capped copy
sales["amount_capped"] = sales["amount"].clip(upper=upper_bound)
print(sales[["order_id", "amount", "amount_capped"]])

blocks.text: Same detection rule flagged both rows. Completely different handling, because the two numbers meant completely different things. That gap between what a statistical rule flags and what you actually do about it is the entire point of this lesson.
8. Summary and What Comes Next
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417252-586438759.png

items: The IQR rule flags anything below Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR, the same rule a box plot draws as its whiskers.
The z-score rule flags anything with an absolute z-score above roughly 3, meaning more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.
Z-score has a circularity problem: the mean and standard deviation it depends on are themselves sensitive to the very outliers you are trying to find.
The two methods can disagree, and when they do, it is usually because one extreme value has already distorted the mean and standard deviation that z-score relies on.
Detection only produces a candidate. Deciding whether it is a genuine rare event or a data entry error requires domain knowledge, not just a formula.
Once confirmed, you can remove the row, cap it with clip, or leave it alone and switch to a model or preprocessing step that is naturally robust to extremes.

blocks.text: The next lesson in this module, encoding categories, moves from numeric columns to categorical ones, but the underlying theme carries over directly: real data is messy, and the tools you reach for depend on what that messiness actually means, not just on what a formula flags.
